from datetime import date

import pytest

from datewise import parse_date

BASE = date(2026, 10, 2)  # a Friday


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "text, expected",
    [
        ("the first Monday of next month", date(2026, 11, 2)),
        ("first monday of this month", date(2026, 10, 5)),
        ("last Friday of next month", date(2026, 11, 27)),
        ("2nd Tuesday of March", date(2027, 3, 9)),
        ("third Thursday in November 2026", date(2026, 11, 19)),
        ("the last sunday of the month after next", date(2026, 12, 27)),
    ],
)
def test_nth_weekday(text, expected):
    assert parse_date(text, BASE) == expected


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "text, expected",
    [
        ("tomorrow", date(2026, 10, 3)),
        ("3 days ago", date(2026, 9, 29)),
        ("in 2 weeks", date(2026, 10, 16)),
        ("March 5th 2027", date(2027, 3, 5)),
        ("2026-12-25", date(2026, 12, 25)),
    ],
)
def test_freeform(text, expected):
    assert parse_date(text, BASE) == expected


def test_no_fifth_weekday():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        parse_date("fifth Monday of next month", BASE)  # Nov 2026 has 5? no: 2,9,16,23,30

# datewise

Parse flexible, human-written date strings into dates.

```sh
uv run datewise the first Monday of next month          # 2026-11-02
uv run datewise "last friday of February 2027"          # 2027-02-26
uv run datewise --base 2026-01-15 "3 days ago"          # 2026-01-12
```

```python
from datewise import parse_date
parse_date("2nd Tuesday of March")
```

- **Nth-weekday expressions** ("first/2nd/.../last <weekday> of <month>") are
  handled in-house with `dateutil.relativedelta`. `<month>` can be `this/next/last
  month`, `month after next`, a month name (next occurrence), or `March 2027`.
- **Everything else** ("tomorrow", "in 2 weeks", "Dec 25", ISO dates) goes to
  [`dateparser`](https://dateparser.readthedocs.io/), preferring future dates.

Run tests: `uv run pytest`
EOF

I've set up a uv-managed Python 3.13 project called `datewise` in `/work`. It parses "the first Monday of next month" correctly (2026-11-02), and all 12 tests pass.

**Layout**
- `pyproject.toml`: depends on `dateparser` and `python-dateutil`, with `pytest` as a dev dependency. It also defines a `datewise` command.
- `src/datewise/__init__.py`: `parse_date(text, base=None) -> date` plus the command-line entry point.
- `tests/test_datewise.py`: tests run against a fixed reference date, so they don't depend on today's date.
- `README.md`, `.gitignore`, `uv.lock`

**How it works**
- **General phrases** like "tomorrow", "in 2 weeks" or "March 5th 2027" are handled by `dateparser`. When a phrase is ambiguous it picks the future date, and relative phrases are counted from a reference date you can set (`--base` on the command line, `base` in Python).
- **"Nth weekday of a month" phrases** (first/2nd/…/last + weekday + "of" or "in" + a month) need their own code, because `dateparser` can't parse them. They're handled with a regex plus `relativedelta`, which is what `dateutil` provides for this kind of date arithmetic. The month can be "this/next/last month", "month after next", a month name on its own, or a month with a year like "March 2027". If the date doesn't exist, it raises `ValueError` — for example, December 2026 has only four Mondays.

```sh
uv run datewise the first Monday of next month     # 2026-11-02
uv run datewise "last friday of February 2027"     # 2027-02-26
uv run pytest
```

**Limitations**
- Other kinds of date arithmetic, such as "the weekday after the 15th" or "2 business days after X", aren't supported yet. New phrase types can be added the same way as the Nth-weekday ones.
- A month name on its own means its next occurrence, counting the current month. So "first Monday of October" today gives October 5, 2026, not a date in 2027.

Nothing is committed yet.
